es.title: Brecha de Amadeus: aerolíneas afectadas y qué hacer si has volado
es.description: Un acceso no autorizado a Amadeus, el proveedor español de reservas, ha expuesto datos de pasajeros de Japan Airlines, ANA, Cathay Pacific, Singapore Airlines y otras. No consta acceso a tarjetas. El riesgo real son los correos falsos que conocen tu vuelo.
es.seoDescription: Brecha de Amadeus: JAL, ANA, Cathay y Singapore Airlines avisan de datos de reservas expuestos. Qué se sabe y qué hacer si has volado.
es.body:
Un acceso no autorizado a los sistemas de Amadeus, la empresa con [sede en Madrid](https://www.muyseguridad.net/2026/11/05/la-brecha-de-amadeus-expone-datos-de-reserva-de-grandes-aerolineas-asiaticas/) que da tecnología de reservas, billetes y facturación a [más de 400 aerolíneas](https://bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/japan-airlines-suffers-third-party-data-breach-exposing-passenger-info), ha dejado expuestos datos de pasajeros de varias compañías. [Singapore Airlines fue la última en contarlo, el 3 de noviembre](https://www.thestar.com.my/business/business-news/2026/11/04/singapore-airlines-says-46000-booking-records-affected-by-amadeus-breach), con unos 46.000 registros de reserva. Amadeus [asegura](https://amadeus.com/amadeus-statement-oct) que no hay pruebas de acceso a datos de pago y que la investigación sigue abierta.

Si has reservado un vuelo con alguna de estas aerolíneas en los últimos tres años, tu tarjeta no parece ser el problema. Lo que debería preocuparte es recibir un correo que conozca tu vuelo.

## Qué ha pasado

Amadeus ha contado muy poco, así que la cronología hay que montarla con lo que dicen otros:

- 21 de septiembre: Amadeus recibe el aviso de una posible vulnerabilidad en un "entorno de visualización" de reservas, según [le dijo a heise](https://www.heise.de/en/news/Security-vulnerability-in-flight-booking-system-11485328.html).
- 24 de septiembre: Amadeus detecta el acceso no autorizado y no avisa a ANA ese día, según [la cronología de la aerolínea](https://www.traicy.com/?p=386421).
- 1 de octubre: Amadeus [publica un comunicado breve](https://bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/japan-airlines-suffers-third-party-data-breach-exposing-passenger-info), sin cifras ni nombres de aerolíneas.
- 13 de octubre: [heise revela](https://www.heise.de/en/news/Security-vulnerability-in-flight-booking-system-11485328.html) que había un volcado de memoria accesible sin autenticación, con credenciales y contraseñas de administrador, y que se podían consultar datos de pasajeros en claro.
- 16 de octubre: ANA se entera por otras aerolíneas y [pregunta a Amadeus](https://www.traicy.com/?p=386421).
- 20 de octubre: Amadeus avisa a ANA, a [Korean Air](https://aviationtoday.in/civilaviation/airlines/airlines-across-asia-and-europe-report-data-exposure-in-amadeus-cybersecurity-incident/) y a [Asiana](https://flyasiana.com/C/KR/KO/customer/notice/detail?id=CM202610230002530882). A [Japan Airlines](https://bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/japan-airlines-suffers-third-party-data-breach-exposing-passenger-info) le llega el aviso el 23 y a [Cathay Pacific](https://www.cathaypacific.com/cx/en_US/latest-news/security-and-operational-changes/personal-data-security.html) el 28.

## Qué aerolíneas están afectadas y qué datos

Esto es lo que han publicado hasta hoy:

- Japan Airlines y Japan Transocean Air: [unos 92.000 clientes](https://bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/japan-airlines-suffers-third-party-data-breach-exposing-passenger-info). En unos 2.000 casos hay también correo, teléfono, pasaporte y nacionalidad.
- Cathay Pacific: [unas 53.000 reservas](https://www.cathaypacific.com/cx/en_US/latest-news/security-and-operational-changes/personal-data-security.html). En una parte menor, además, contacto, documento de viaje o número de viajero frecuente.
- Singapore Airlines: [unos 46.000 registros](https://www.thestar.com.my/business/business-news/2026/11/04/singapore-airlines-says-46000-booking-records-affected-by-amadeus-breach), unos 620 de ellos con correo, teléfono y documento de viaje.
- ANA: [unos 37.800 clientes](https://aviationtoday.in/civilaviation/airlines/airlines-across-asia-and-europe-report-data-exposure-in-amadeus-cybersecurity-incident/), unos 1.700 con datos adicionales como el pasaporte. Star Flyer, Air Do y Solaseed Air también han avisado, tras saberlo por ANA.
- [Korean Air](https://aviationtoday.in/civilaviation/airlines/airlines-across-asia-and-europe-report-data-exposure-in-amadeus-cybersecurity-incident/) y [Asiana](https://flyasiana.com/C/KR/KO/customer/notice/detail?id=CM202610230002530882): números de reserva de algunos clientes, sin cifra total.
- [Malaysia Airlines](https://www.malaysiaairlines.com/my/en/mh-media-centre/important-for-you/cybersecurity-incident-third-party-technology-provider.html): dice que algunos datos pueden estar afectados, sin cifra.
- Condor: [lo ha confirmado a la prensa alemana](https://www.touristik-aktuell.de/verkehr/amadeus-datenleck-airlines/), sin cifra.
- Qantas: [sigue comprobando](https://www.ibtimes.co.uk/amadeus-breach-exposes-airline-booking-data-1829581) si hay reservas suyas.

Estas cifras no se pueden sumar, porque unas cuentan clientes y otras reservas. Amadeus [no ha querido decir](https://therecord.media/asian-airlines-announce-data-breach-it-provider-incident) cuántas víctimas hay en total.

En la mayoría de los casos lo expuesto es nombre, localizador y datos del vuelo. [Japan Airlines y ANA](https://aviationtoday.in/civilaviation/airlines/airlines-across-asia-and-europe-report-data-exposure-in-amadeus-cybersecurity-incident/) dicen que no hay tarjetas ni contraseñas, y Cathay, que [no hay pruebas](https://www.cathaypacific.com/cx/en_US/latest-news/security-and-operational-changes/personal-data-security.html) de acceso a datos financieros.

¿Y las aerolíneas españolas? No he encontrado ningún aviso de Iberia, Vueling o Air Europa, [igual que MuySeguridad](https://www.muyseguridad.net/2026/11/05/la-brecha-de-amadeus-expone-datos-de-reserva-de-grandes-aerolineas-asiaticas/), ni ningún anuncio de la AEPD sobre este caso. Eso no significa que estén a salvo: la lista ha ido creciendo y Amadeus no ha dicho si está cerrada.

## Lo que no se sabe

Cómo entraron. Amadeus [habla de una vulnerabilidad](https://amadeus.com/amadeus-statement-oct), mientras que [Cathay](https://www.cathaypacific.com/cx/en_US/latest-news/security-and-operational-changes/personal-data-security.html) y [Asiana](https://flyasiana.com/C/KR/KO/customer/notice/detail?id=CM202610230002530882) hablan de credenciales de una cuenta del propio sistema. El volcado que encontró heise contenía credenciales, y la tentación de unir las dos cosas es grande, pero ninguna fuente oficial lo ha confirmado y yo tampoco lo doy por hecho.

Quién fue. Nadie lo ha atribuido a un grupo o a un país, y Amadeus [no aclara](https://therecord.media/asian-airlines-announce-data-breach-it-provider-incident) si los atacantes se han puesto en contacto con la empresa.

Cuánto duró. Varias dan un periodo de agosto de 2023 a septiembre de 2026, pero no significa lo mismo en cada aviso. Cathay lo presenta como [cuándo ocurrió el acceso](https://www.cathaypacific.com/cx/en_US/latest-news/security-and-operational-changes/personal-data-security.html), ANA como [las fechas en que se hicieron las reservas](https://aviationtoday.in/civilaviation/airlines/airlines-across-asia-and-europe-report-data-exposure-in-amadeus-cybersecurity-incident/) y Asiana [advierte](https://flyasiana.com/C/KR/KO/customer/notice/detail?id=CM202610230002530882) de que el momento exacto sigue en investigación. Así que todavía no se puede afirmar que alguien estuviera dentro tres años.

Si se han usado los datos. [Según Cathay](https://www.cathaypacific.com/cx/en_US/latest-news/security-and-operational-changes/personal-data-security.html), Amadeus no ha visto indicios de uso indebido. Eso es lo que se sabe hoy, y no dice nada de lo que pueda pasar con esos datos mañana.

## ¿Para qué sirve un localizador robado?

Sirve sobre todo para engañarte. Imagina que te llega un correo con tu nombre, tu localizador y tu vuelo del jueves a Tokio, que te pide confirmar el pasaporte o pagar un suplemento antes de facturar. Normalmente esos datos serían la prueba de que el mensaje es de verdad. Después de una brecha así, dejan de serlo.

Además, en muchas aerolíneas el localizador y el apellido bastan para abrir una reserva en su web. Por eso [Singapore Airlines está contactando](https://www.thestar.com.my/business/business-news/2026/11/04/singapore-airlines-says-46000-booking-records-affected-by-amadeus-breach) con quienes tienen viajes próximos para cambiarles el localizador.

## Qué hacer si has volado con estas aerolíneas

- Entra en la web de la aerolínea escribiendo tú la dirección, busca su aviso y revisa tus reservas futuras.
- Desconfía de cualquier mensaje que mencione tu vuelo y te pida dinero, la tarjeta o el documento, aunque los datos sean correctos. Aquí tienes [cómo reconocer un correo de phishing](/es/blog/como-saber-si-un-correo-es-phishing).
- Ante la duda, llama al número que aparece en la web oficial, nunca al que venga en el mensaje.
- Si tienes un vuelo próximo, pregunta si pueden cambiarte el localizador.
- Si te avisan de que tu pasaporte estaba entre los datos, guarda el aviso y pregunta a la aerolínea qué recomienda.
- Si tienes dudas sobre un mensaje, el [017 de INCIBE](https://www.incibe.es/linea-de-ayuda-en-ciberseguridad) es gratuito y confidencial.

## Qué debería mirar una empresa

Si tu plantilla viaja, avísala. El itinerario de un directivo es muy útil para quien prepara un [fraude del CEO](/es/blog/fraude-del-ceo-como-detectarlo): saber que está en un avión es saber que no va a coger el teléfono.

Fíjate también en que las aerolíneas [repiten que sus sistemas no se han visto afectados](https://therecord.media/asian-airlines-announce-data-breach-it-provider-incident). Es lo que dicen sus avisos, pero los datos de sus clientes estaban en casa del proveedor. Tu empresa tiene el mismo problema con su gestoría, su CRM o su proveedor de nóminas.

Por eso conviene mirar qué dice tu contrato sobre los avisos. El [artículo 33 del RGPD](https://www.boe.es/buscar/doc.php?id=DOUE-L-2016-80807) obliga al encargado a notificar al responsable sin dilación indebida, y al responsable a avisar a la autoridad, si es posible, en 72 horas desde que tiene constancia. Con [la cronología de ANA](https://www.traicy.com/?p=386421), entre la detección y su aviso pasaron 26 días. No digo que Amadeus haya incumplido nada: no sé cuándo supo qué datos eran de quién, y no conozco ninguna resolución al respecto. Lo que digo es que tu plan de respuesta no puede depender de que el proveedor avise rápido.

Si tienes equipo técnico, hay dos deberes claros. Las cuentas de sistema necesitan rotación de contraseñas, permisos mínimos y alertas cuando hacen algo raro. Y si usáis Spring Boot, comprobad que el endpoint `heapdump` no esté abierto a internet: heise no dice qué endpoint era exactamente, pero [la documentación oficial](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/reference/actuator/endpoints.html) lo deja restringido por defecto, así que abrirlo es una decisión que alguien toma.

Actualizaré este artículo cuando Amadeus o las aerolíneas den más datos. Y si quieres que tu plantilla sepa reaccionar a un correo que conoce su vuelo, es justo lo que trabajo en mis [formaciones de ciberseguridad](/es/training).

en.title: Amadeus data breach: affected airlines and what passengers should do
en.description: Unauthorized access to Amadeus, the Spanish booking technology provider, has exposed passenger data from Japan Airlines, ANA, Cathay Pacific, Singapore Airlines and others. There's no sign of card data being accessed. The real risk is fake emails that know your flight.
en.seoDescription: Amadeus data breach: JAL, ANA, Cathay and Singapore Airlines report exposed booking data. What's known and what to do if you've flown.
en.body:
Unauthorized access to systems at Amadeus, the [Madrid-based](https://www.muyseguridad.net/2026/11/05/la-brecha-de-amadeus-expone-datos-de-reserva-de-grandes-aerolineas-asiaticas/) company that supplies reservation, ticketing and check-in technology to [more than 400 airlines](https://bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/japan-airlines-suffers-third-party-data-breach-exposing-passenger-info), has exposed passenger data from several carriers. [Singapore Airlines was the latest to disclose it, on November 3](https://www.thestar.com.my/business/business-news/2026/11/04/singapore-airlines-says-46000-booking-records-affected-by-amadeus-breach), with about 46,000 booking records. Amadeus [says](https://amadeus.com/amadeus-statement-oct) there is no evidence that payment data was accessed and that its investigation continues.

If you booked with one of these airlines in the last three years, your card is probably not the problem. The thing to watch for is an email that already knows your flight.

## What happened

Amadeus has said very little, so the timeline has to be pieced together from other sources:

- September 21: Amadeus is told of a potential vulnerability in a booking "display environment", according to [what it told heise](https://www.heise.de/en/news/Security-vulnerability-in-flight-booking-system-11485328.html).
- September 24: Amadeus detects the unauthorized access but doesn't tell ANA that day, according to [the airline's timeline](https://www.traicy.com/?p=386421).
- October 1: Amadeus [publishes a short statement](https://bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/japan-airlines-suffers-third-party-data-breach-exposing-passenger-info) with no figures and no airline names.
- October 13: [heise reports](https://www.heise.de/en/news/Security-vulnerability-in-flight-booking-system-11485328.html) a memory dump reachable without authentication, holding credentials and admin passwords, and says passenger data could be viewed in plain text.
- October 16: ANA hears about it from other airlines and [asks Amadeus](https://www.traicy.com/?p=386421).
- October 20: Amadeus notifies ANA, [Korean Air](https://aviationtoday.in/civilaviation/airlines/airlines-across-asia-and-europe-report-data-exposure-in-amadeus-cybersecurity-incident/) and [Asiana](https://flyasiana.com/C/KR/KO/customer/notice/detail?id=CM202610230002530882). [Japan Airlines](https://bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/japan-airlines-suffers-third-party-data-breach-exposing-passenger-info) gets the notice on the 23rd and [Cathay Pacific](https://www.cathaypacific.com/cx/en_US/latest-news/security-and-operational-changes/personal-data-security.html) on the 28th.

## Which airlines are affected, and what data

This is what has been published so far:

- Japan Airlines and Japan Transocean Air: [about 92,000 customers](https://bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/japan-airlines-suffers-third-party-data-breach-exposing-passenger-info). About 2,000 cases also include email, phone, passport and nationality.
- Cathay Pacific: [about 53,000 bookings](https://www.cathaypacific.com/cx/en_US/latest-news/security-and-operational-changes/personal-data-security.html). A smaller subset also includes contact details, travel documents or frequent flyer numbers.
- Singapore Airlines: [about 46,000 records](https://www.thestar.com.my/business/business-news/2026/11/04/singapore-airlines-says-46000-booking-records-affected-by-amadeus-breach), around 620 of them with email, phone and travel document details.
- ANA: [about 37,800 customers](https://aviationtoday.in/civilaviation/airlines/airlines-across-asia-and-europe-report-data-exposure-in-amadeus-cybersecurity-incident/), around 1,700 with extra data such as passport numbers. Star Flyer, Air Do and Solaseed Air have also issued notices after hearing from ANA.
- [Korean Air](https://aviationtoday.in/civilaviation/airlines/airlines-across-asia-and-europe-report-data-exposure-in-amadeus-cybersecurity-incident/) and [Asiana](https://flyasiana.com/C/KR/KO/customer/notice/detail?id=CM202610230002530882): booking numbers for some customers, no total given.
- [Malaysia Airlines](https://www.malaysiaairlines.com/my/en/mh-media-centre/important-for-you/cybersecurity-incident-third-party-technology-provider.html): says some customer data may be affected, no figure.
- Condor: [has confirmed it to the German press](https://www.touristik-aktuell.de/verkehr/amadeus-datenleck-airlines/), no figure.
- Qantas: [still checking](https://www.ibtimes.co.uk/amadeus-breach-exposes-airline-booking-data-1829581) whether its bookings are involved.

These numbers can't be added up, because some count customers and others count bookings. Amadeus [declined to say](https://therecord.media/asian-airlines-announce-data-breach-it-provider-incident) how many victims there are overall.

In most cases the exposed data is a name, a booking reference and flight details. [Japan Airlines and ANA](https://aviationtoday.in/civilaviation/airlines/airlines-across-asia-and-europe-report-data-exposure-in-amadeus-cybersecurity-incident/) say no card numbers or passwords were involved, and Cathay says there is [no evidence](https://www.cathaypacific.com/cx/en_US/latest-news/security-and-operational-changes/personal-data-security.html) of access to financial data.

What about Spanish airlines? I couldn't find any notice from Iberia, Vueling or Air Europa, [nor could MuySeguridad](https://www.muyseguridad.net/2026/11/05/la-brecha-de-amadeus-expone-datos-de-reserva-de-grandes-aerolineas-asiaticas/), and I found no announcement from Spain's data protection agency about this case. That doesn't mean they're in the clear: the list has kept growing, and Amadeus hasn't said whether it's complete.

## What we don't know

How they got in. Amadeus [talks about a vulnerability](https://amadeus.com/amadeus-statement-oct), while [Cathay](https://www.cathaypacific.com/cx/en_US/latest-news/security-and-operational-changes/personal-data-security.html) and [Asiana](https://flyasiana.com/C/KR/KO/customer/notice/detail?id=CM202610230002530882) talk about login credentials for an account on its own system. The dump heise found contained credentials, and it's tempting to connect the two, but no official source has confirmed that and I won't assume it either.

Who did it. Nobody has attributed this to a group or a country, and Amadeus [won't say](https://therecord.media/asian-airlines-announce-data-breach-it-provider-incident) whether the attackers have contacted the company.

How long it lasted. Several give a period from August 2023 to September 2026, but it doesn't mean the same thing in each notice. Cathay presents it as [when the access happened](https://www.cathaypacific.com/cx/en_US/latest-news/security-and-operational-changes/personal-data-security.html), ANA as [when the bookings were made](https://aviationtoday.in/civilaviation/airlines/airlines-across-asia-and-europe-report-data-exposure-in-amadeus-cybersecurity-incident/), and Asiana [warns](https://flyasiana.com/C/KR/KO/customer/notice/detail?id=CM202610230002530882) that the exact timing is still under investigation. So nobody can yet say that someone was inside for three years.

Whether the data has been used. [According to Cathay](https://www.cathaypacific.com/cx/en_US/latest-news/security-and-operational-changes/personal-data-security.html), Amadeus has found no evidence of misuse. That's where things stand today, and it says nothing about what could happen to the data tomorrow.

## What can someone do with a stolen booking reference?

Mostly, fool you. Imagine an email with your name, your booking reference and your Thursday flight to Tokyo, asking you to confirm your passport or pay a surcharge before check-in. Normally those details would prove the message was real. After a breach like this, they don't.

On many airlines, the booking reference and surname are also enough to open a booking on the website. That's why [Singapore Airlines is contacting](https://www.thestar.com.my/business/business-news/2026/11/04/singapore-airlines-says-46000-booking-records-affected-by-amadeus-breach) customers with upcoming trips to change their booking references.

## What to do if you've flown with these airlines

- Type the airline's address yourself, look for its notice and check your upcoming bookings.
- Be wary of any message that mentions your flight and asks for money, your card or your ID, even if the details are right. Here's [how to spot a phishing email](/en/blog/how-to-spot-a-phishing-email).
- If in doubt, call the number on the official website, never the one in the message.
- If you have a flight coming up, ask whether they can change your booking reference.
- If you're told your passport was among the data, keep the notice and ask the airline what it recommends.
- In Spain, [INCIBE's 017 helpline](https://www.incibe.es/linea-de-ayuda-en-ciberseguridad) is free and confidential if you're unsure about a message.

## What a company should check

If your staff travel, warn them. An executive's itinerary is very useful to anyone preparing [CEO fraud](/en/blog/ceo-fraud-how-to-spot-it): knowing they're on a plane means knowing they won't pick up the phone.

Notice too that the airlines [keep saying their own systems weren't affected](https://therecord.media/asian-airlines-announce-data-breach-it-provider-incident). That's what their notices say, but their customers' data was sitting with the supplier. Your company has the same exposure with its accountants, its CRM or its payroll provider.

So it's worth checking what your contract says about notification. [Article 33 of the GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj) requires a processor to notify the controller without undue delay, and the controller to notify the authority, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware. On [ANA's timeline](https://www.traicy.com/?p=386421), 26 days passed between detection and its notice. I'm not saying Amadeus broke any rule: I don't know when it learned whose data was involved, and I'm not aware of any ruling on this. My point is that your response plan can't depend on your supplier telling you quickly.

If you have a technical team, there are two clear jobs. System accounts need password rotation, least privilege and alerts for unusual activity. And if you use Spring Boot, check that the `heapdump` endpoint isn't open to the internet: heise doesn't say exactly which endpoint this was, but [the official documentation](https://docs.spring.io/spring-boot/reference/actuator/endpoints.html) keeps it restricted by default, so opening it is a decision somebody makes.

I'll update this article when Amadeus or the airlines share more. And if you'd like your team to know how to react to an email that knows their flight, that's what I work on in my [cybersecurity training](/en/training).
